text.uk: Майстер мовив: «Ти сниш, що ти метелик. А потім прокидаєшся. Чи певен ти, що не є метеликом, якому сниться, що він людина?»

author: Buddha
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 33 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

title.fr: Sans mot et sans absence de mots

text.en: Nansen said: "Mind is not Buddha. Learning is not the path."
text.fr:
Un philosophe demanda au Bouddha :

Sans mot et sans absence de mots, peux-tu me dire la vérité ?

Le Bouddha garda le silence.

Alors le philosophe s’inclina respectueusement et remercia le Bouddha :

Par ta compassion j’ai dissipé mes illusions et j’ai atteint la vraie voie.

Plus tard, Ananda demanda au Bouddha ce que le philosophe avait atteint. Le Bouddha répondit :
La seule ombre d’un fouet fait galoper un bon cheval.
text.ja: 南泉云く、「心は是れ佛にあらず、智は是れ道にあらず。」 無門曰く、「南泉謂つべし、老いて羞を識らずと。纔かに臭口を開けば家醜外に揚がる。是の如くなりと然雖も、恩を知る者は少し。」 頌に曰く、 天睛れて日頭出で、雨下って地上濕う。 情を盡して都べて説き了る、只だ恐らくは信不及なることを。
text.uk: Ріка тече до океану. Коли вона досягає океану, вона все ще вода. Та вона вже не ріка.

author: Nansen
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 34 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en: "Seijo, the Chinese girl," observed Goso, "had two souls, one always sick at home and the other in the city, a married woman with two children. Which was the true soul?"
text.fr:
Un moine demanda à Baso :

Qu’est-ce que le Bouddha ?

Baso répondit :

L’esprit n’est pas le Bouddha !
text.ja: 五祖、僧に問うて云く、「倩女離魂、那箇か是れ眞底。」 無門曰く、「若し者裏に向って眞底を悟り得ば、便ち知らん殼を出でて殼に入ること、旅舍に宿するが如くなるを。其れ或は未だ然らずんば、切に亂走すること莫れ。驀然として地水火風一散せば、湯に落つる螃蟹の七手八脚なるが如くならん。那時言うことなかれ、道わずと。」 頌に曰く、 雲月是れ同じ、溪山各各異なり。 萬福萬福、是れ一か是れ二か。
text.uk: Майстер запалив пахощі. Коли дим піднявся, він мовив: «Оце вчення. Воно віддає себе повністю і нічого не просить.»

author: Seijo
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 35 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

title.en: Meeting a Zen Master on the Road

text.en: Goso said: "When you meet a Zen master on the road you cannot talk to him, you cannot face him with silence. What are you going to do?"
text.fr:
Nansen dit :

L’esprit n’est pas le Bouddha !… et apprendre n’est pas la voie !
text.ja: 五祖曰く、「路に達道の人に逢わば、語默を將って對せず。且らく道え、甚麼を將ってか對せん。」 無門曰く、「若し者裏に向って對得して親切ならば、妨げず慶快なることを。其れ或は未だ然らずんば、也た須らく一切處に眼を著くべし。」 頌に曰く、 路に達道の人に逢わば、語默を將って對せず。 攔腮劈面に拳す、直下に會せば便ち會す。
text.uk: Коли ставок спокійний, він віддзеркалює все досконало. Коли брижі — нічого не видно. Нехай твій розум буде тихим ставком.

author: Goso
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 36 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

title.en: A Buffalo Passes Through the Enclosure

text.en: Goso said: "When a buffalo goes out of his enclosure to the edge of the abyss, his horns and his head and his hoofs all pass through, but why can't the tail also pass?"
text.fr:
Goso se posa la question suivante :

La jeune chinoise Seijô a deux âmes. L’une est chez elle, toujours malade. L’autre est à la ville, mariée, avec deux enfants. Laquelle est la véritable âme de Seijô ?
text.ja: 趙州、因みに僧問う、「如何なるか是れ祖師西來の意。」州云く、「庭前の柏樹子。」 無門曰く、「若し趙州の答處に向って見得して親切ならば、前に釋迦無く、後に彌勒無し。」 頌に曰く、 言、事を展ぶること無く、語、機に投ぜず。 言を承くる者は喪し、句に滯る者は迷う。
text.uk:
Монах спитав: «Яке найглибше вчення?»
Майстер мовив: «Стара криниця, якою ніколи не користувались.»

author: Goso
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 37 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

title.en: An Oak Tree in the Garden

text.en:
A monk asked Joshu why Bodhidharma came to China. 

Joshu said: "An oak tree in the garden."
text.fr:
Goso posa la question suivante :

Quand tu rencontres un maître sur ton chemin, tu ne peux pas lui parler… mais tu ne peux pas non plus le regarder en silence. Alors que fais-tu ?
text.ja: 五祖曰く、「譬えば水牯牛の窓櫺を過ぐるが如き、頭角四蹄都べて過ぎ了るに、甚麼に因ってか尾巴過ぐることを得ざる。」 無門曰く、「若し者裏に向って顛倒して、一隻眼を著け得、一轉語を下し得ば、以て上四恩に報じ、下三有を資くべし。其れ或は未だ然らずんば、更に須らく尾巴を照顧して始めて得べし。」 頌に曰く、 過ぎ去れば坑壍に墮ち、囘り來れば却って壞らる。 者些の尾巴子、直に是れ甚だ奇怪なり。
text.uk: Майстер мовив: «Слива цвіте в зимовому снігу. Вона не чекає весни.»

author: Joshu
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 38 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
A Zen student told Ummon: "Brilliancy of Buddha illuminates the whole universe."

Before he finished the phrase Ummon asked: "You are reciting another's poem, are you not?"

"Yes," answered the student.

"You are sidetracked," said Ummon.

Afterwards another teacher, Shishin, asked his pupils: "At what point did that student go off the track?"
text.fr:
Goso se posa la question suivante :

Lorsqu’un buffle s’échappe de son enclos pour se précipiter vers le bord d’un ravin, ses cornes passent, sa tête passe, ses sabots passent, tout passe… sauf la queue. Pourquoi la queue ne peut-elle pas passer ?
text.ja: 雲門、因みに僧問う、「光明寂照遍河沙。」一句未だ絶せざるに門遽かに曰く、「豈に是れ張拙秀才の語にあらずや。」僧云く、「是。」門云く、「話墮せり。」後來、死心拈じて云く、「且らく道え、那裏か是れ者の僧が話墮の處。」 無門曰く、「若し者裏に向って雲門の用處孤危、者の僧甚に因ってか話墮すと見得せば、人天の與に師と爲るに堪えん。若也未だ明らめずんば、自救不了。」 頌に曰く、 急流に釣を垂る、餌を貪る者は著く。 口縫纔かに開けば、性命喪却せん。
text.uk: Майстер мовив: «Гірська стежка крута й вузька. Та кожен крок — вершина.»

author: Ummon
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 39 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
Hyakujo wished to send a monk to open a new monastery. He told his pupils that whoever answered a question most ably would be appointed. Placing a water vase on the ground, he asked: "Who can say what this is without calling its name?"

The chief monk said: "No one can call it a wooden shoe."

Isan, the cooking monk, tipped over the vase with his foot and went out.

Hyakujo smiled and said: "The chief monk loses." And Isan became the master of the new monastery.
text.fr:
Un jour, un moine demanda à Joshu :

Pourquoi Boddhidharma est-il venu en Chine ?

À cela, Joshu répondit :

Un chêne dans le jardin !
text.ja: 潙山和尚、始め百丈の會中に在って典座に充たる。百丈將に大潙の主人を選ばんとす。乃ち請じて首座と同じく衆に對して下語せしめ、出格の者往く可しと。百丈遂に淨瓶を拈じて、地上に置いて問を設けて云く、「喚んで淨瓶と作すことを得ず、汝喚んで甚麼とか作さん。」首座乃ち云く、「喚んで木𣔻と作す可からず。」百丈却って山に問う。山乃ち淨瓶を趯倒して去る。百丈笑って云く、「第一座、山子に輸却せらる」と。因って之に命じて開山と爲す。 無門曰く、「潙山一期の勇、爭奈せん百丈の圏圚を跳り出でざることを。檢點し將ち來れば、重きに便りして輕きに便りせず。何が故ぞ、聻。盤頭を脱得して鐵枷を擔起す。」 頌に曰く、 笊籬并びに木杓を颺下して、當陽の一突周遮を絶す。 百丈の重關も攔り住めず、脚尖潙出して、佛麻の如し。
text.uk:
Монах спитав: «Який сенс у монашій робі?»
Майстер мовив: «Вона нічого не вкриває і все відкриває.»

author: Hyakujo
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 40 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
Bodhidharma sits facing the wall. His future successor stands in the snow and presents his severed  arm to Bodhidharma. He cries: "My mind is not pacified. Master, pacify my mind."

Bodhidharma says: "If you bring me that mind, I will pacify it for you."

The successor says: "When I search my mind I cannot hold it."

Bodhidharma says: "Then your mind is pacified already."
text.fr:
Un disciple dit un jour à Ummon :

L’éclat du Bouddha illumine tout l’Univers.

Aussitôt, Ummon demanda :

Tu récites le poème de quelqu’un d’autre, n’est-ce pas ?

Oui.

Tu as quitté ta voie !!!

Plus tard Shishin, un autre maître, demanda à ses élèves :

À quel moment ce disciple a t’il quitté la voie ?
text.ja: 達磨面壁す。二祖雪に立つ。臂を斷って云く、「弟子は心未だ安からず、乞う師安心せしめよ。」磨云く、「心を將ち來れ、汝が爲めに安んぜん。」祖云く、「心を覓むるに了に不可得なり。」磨云く、「汝が爲めに安心し竟んぬ。」 無門曰く、「缺齒の老胡、十萬里の海を航して特特として來る。謂つべし是れ風無きに浪を起すと。末後に一箇の門人を接得して、又た却って六根不具。咦、謝三郎四字を識らず。」 頌に曰く、 西來の直指、事は囑するに因って起る。 叢林を撓聒するは、元來是れ儞。
text.uk:
Монах спитав: «Що таке великий океан просвітлення?»
Майстер мовив: «Він не далеко, не близько. Не великий, не малий.»

author: Bodhidharma
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 41 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

title.en: The Girl Comes Out from Meditation

text.en:
In the time of Buddha Shakyamuni, Manjusri went to the assemblage of the Buddhas. When he arrived there, the conference was over and each Buddha had returned to his own Buddha-land. Only one girl was yet unmoved in deep meditation.

Manjusri asked Buddha Shakyamuni how it was possible for this girl to reach this state, one which even he could not attain. "Bring her out  from Samadhi and ask her yourself," said the Buddha.

Manjusri walked around the girl three times and snapped his fingers. She still remained in meditation. So by his miracle power he transported her to a high heaven and tried his best to call her, but in vain.

Buddha Shakyamuni said: "Even a hundred thousand Manjusris could not disturb her, but below this place, past twelve hundred million countries, is a Bodhisattva, Mo-myo, seed of delusion. If he comes here, she will awaken."

No sooner had the Buddha spoken than that Bodhisattva sprang up from the earth and bowed and paid homage to the Buddha. Buddha directed him to arouse the girl. The Bodhisattva went in front of the girl and snapped his fingers, and in that instant the girl came out from her deep meditation.
text.fr:
Hyakujô cherchait un moine capable de diriger un nouveau monastère. Il dit à ses élèves que celui d’entre eux qui répondrait la mieux à une question serait désigné.

Il plaça une cruche pleine d’eau au sol au milieu de la pièce et demanda :

Qui peut me dire ce qu’est ceci, à part me dire que c’est une cruche ?

Le moine Supérieur se risqua :

Personne ne pourrait dire que c’est une sandale de bois !

Isan, le simple moine cuisinier, ne dit rien. Il renversa la cruche… et sortit !

Hyakujô sourit et dit au moine Supérieur :

Tu as perdu !

Isan fut nommé maître du nouveau monastère.
text.ja: 世尊、昔、因みに文殊、諸佛の集る處に至って、諸佛各各本處に還るに値う。惟だ一りの女人有って、彼の佛坐に近づいて三昧に入る。文殊乃ち佛に白さく、「云何ぞ女人は佛坐に近づくを得て、我は得ざる。」佛、文殊に告ぐ、「汝但だ此の女を覺して三昧より起たしめて、汝自から之を問え。」文殊、女人を遶ること三匝、指を鳴らすこと一下して、乃ち托して梵天に至って、其の神力を盡すも出だすこと能わず。世尊云く、「假使い百千の文殊も亦た此の女人を定より出だすことを得ず。下方一十二億河沙の國土を過ぎて、罔明菩薩有り。能く此の女人を定より出ださん。」須臾に罔明大士、地より湧出して世尊を禮拜す。世尊、罔明に敕す。却って女人の前に至って指を鳴らすこと一下す。女人是に於て定より出づ。 無門曰く、「釋迦老子、者の一場の雜劇を做す、小小を通ぜず。且らく道え、文殊は是れ七佛の師、甚んに因ってか女人を定より出だすことを得ざる。罔明は初地の菩薩、甚んとしてか却って出だし得る。若し者裏に向って見得して親切ならば、業識忙忙として那伽大定ならん。」 頌に曰く、 出得するも出不得なるも、渠と儂と自由を得たり。 神頭并に鬼面、敗闕當に風流。
text.uk: Майстер увійшов до зали медитації і мовив: «Зала порожня. Монахи сидять. Хто сидить?»

author: Buddha
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 42 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

title.fr: Dialogue entre Boddhidharma et Hui Ko

text.en: Shuzan held out his short staff and said: "If you call this a short staff, you oppose its reality. If you do not call it a short staff, you ignore the fact. Now what do you wish to call this?"
text.fr:
Boddhidharma est assis face au mur. Hui Ko est debout derrière lui dans la neige, se plaignant de la douleur de son bras.

Mon esprit n’est pas en paix, Maître. Je t’en prie, accorde la paix à mon esprit…

Apporte-moi ton esprit, et je le pacifierai pour toi, répond Boddhidharma.

Je cherche mon esprit, Maître… mais je ne peux le trouver.

Alors ton esprit est déjà en paix.
text.ja: 首山和尚、竹箆を拈じて衆に示して云く、「汝等諸人、若し喚んで竹箆と作さば則ち觸る、喚んで竹箆と作さざれば則ち背く。汝諸人、且らく道え、喚んで甚麼とか作さん。」 無門曰く、「喚んで竹箆と作さば、則ち觸る、喚んで竹箆と作さざれば、則ち背く。有語なることを得ず、無語なることを得ず。速かに道え、速かに道え。」 頌に曰く、 竹箆を拈起して、殺活の令を行ず。 背觸交馳、佛祖も命を乞う。
text.uk:
Монах спитав: «Яка щоденна практика ченця дзен?»
Майстер мовив: «Голодний — їж рисову кашу. Втомлений — спи.»

author: Shuzan
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 43 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en: Basho said to his disciple: "When you have a staff, I will give it to you. If you have no staff, I will take it away from you."
text.fr:
Cela se passe à l’époque du Bouddha Shakyâmuni.

Manjushri se rendit à l’assemblée des bouddhas. Quand il arriva là-bas, l’assemblée était finie et chaque bouddha était reparti dans son pays. Tous… sauf une femme qui n’avait pas bougé, restée en profonde méditation.

Manjushri demanda à Shakyamuni :

Comment fait-elle pour atteindre un tel état de méditation ? Moi même j’en suis incapable !

Shakyâmuni répondit :

Sors-la du Samadhi et demande-lui toi même…

Manjushri tourna trois fois autour de la femme puis fit claquer ses doigts. Elle ne bougea pas. Alors par ses pouvoirs extraordinaires il la transporta dans le plus élevé des trois mondes supérieurs et l’appela de toutes ses forces… en vain.

Voyant cela, Shakyâmuni dit :

Cent mille Manjushri ne pourraient la troubler. Mais dans une région profonde, au-dessous des mille deux cent millions de terres, se trouve le plus petit des boddhisattvas, nommé Momyo (Avidya). Il peut la sortir de sa profonde méditation.

Shakyâmuni avait à peine fini de parler que le boddhisattva Momyo apparut, s’inclinant et lui rendant hommage. Shakyâmuni lui demanda de sortir la femme de sa profonde méditation.

Le boddhisattva s’approcha de la femme et fit claquer ses doigts… et la femme sortit de sa profonde méditation.
text.ja: 芭蕉和尚、衆に示して云く、「儞に拄杖子有らば、我れ儞に拄杖子を與えん。儞に拄杖子無くんば、我れ儞が拄杖子を奪わん。」 無門曰く、「扶けては斷橋の水を過ぎ、伴っては無月の村に歸る。若し喚んで拄杖と作さば、地獄に入ること箭の如くならん。」 頌に曰く、 諸方の深と淺と、都べて掌握の中に在り。 天を撐え并びに地を拄えて、隨處に宗風を振う。
text.uk: Монах вичавив мокрий рушник. Майстер мовив: «Тепер він сухий. Він відрізняється від того, яким був до того, як намок?»

author: Basho
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 44 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en: Hoen said: "The past and future Buddhas, both are his servants. Who is he?"
text.fr:
Shuzan montra son kyôsaku aux moines, et dit :

Si vous appelez cela un petit bâton, vous n’exprimez pas la réalité. Si vous ne l’appelez pas un petit bâton vous niez sa nature. Alors… comment appelez-vous ceci ?
text.ja: 東山演師祖曰く、「釋迦彌勒は猶お是れ他の奴。且らく道え、他は是れ阿誰ぞ。」 無門曰く、「若也他を見得して分曉ならば、譬えば十字街頭に親爺に撞見するが如くに相似て、更に別人に問うて是と不是とを道うことを須いず。」 頌に曰く、 他の弓を挽くこと莫れ、他の馬に騎ること莫れ。 他の非を辨ずること莫れ、他の事を知ること莫れ。
text.uk: Майстер мовив: «Твоє життя — немов ткацький верстат. Думки — нитки. Що ти ткаєш?»

author: Buddha
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 45 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

title.en: Proceed from the Top of the Pole

text.en: Sekiso asked: "How can you proceed on from the top of a hundred-foot pole?" Another Zen teacher said: "One who sits on the top of a hundred-foot pole has attained a certain height but still is not handling Zen freely. He should proceed on from there and appear with his whole body in the ten parts of the world."
text.fr:
Bashô dit un jour à son disciple :

Quand tu auras un bâton… je te le donnerai. Mais si tu n’as pas de bâton… je te le retirerai !
text.ja: 石霜和尚曰く、「百尺竿頭、如何が歩を進めん。」又た古徳云く、「百尺竿頭に坐する底の人は、得入すと雖然も、未だ眞と爲さず。百尺竿頭に須らく歩を進めて、十方世界に全身を現ずべし」と。 無門曰く、「歩を進め得、身を翻し得ば、更に何れの處を嫌ってか尊と稱せざる。是の如くなりと雖然も、且らく道え、百尺竿頭如何が歩を進めん。嗄。」 頌に曰く、 頂門の眼を瞎却し、錯って定盤星を認む。 身を𢬵て能く命を捨て、一盲衆盲を引く。
text.uk:
Монах спитав: «Як знайти шлях у темряві?»
Майстер запалив ліхтар і простягнув йому. «Ось», — мовив він.

author: Sekiso
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 46 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
Tosotsu built three barriers and made the monks pass through them. The first barrier is studying Zen. In studying Zen the aim is to see one's own true nature. Now where is your true nature?

Secondly, when one realizes his own true nature he will be free from birth and death. Now when you shut the light from your eyes and become a corpse, how can you free yourself?

Thirdly, if you free yourself from birth and death, you should know where you are. Now your body separates into the four elements. Where are you?
text.fr:
Hôen posa la question suivante :

Les bouddhas du passé et du futur sont tous ses serviteurs… Mais de qui ?
text.ja: 兜率悅和尚、三關を設けて學者に問う、「撥草參玄は只だ見性を圖る。卽今上人の性、甚れの處にか在る。」「自性を識得すれば方に生死を脱す、眼光落つる時作麼生か脱せん。」「生死を脱得すれば便ち去處を知る、四大分離して甚れの處に向ってか去る。」 無門曰く、「若し能く此の三轉語を下し得ば、便ち以って隨處に主と作り、緣に遇うて卽ち宗なるべし。其れ或は未だ然らずんば、麁飡は飽き易く、細嚼は飢え難し。」 頌に曰く、 一念普く觀ず無量劫、無量劫の事卽ち如今。 如今箇の一念を覰破すれば、如今覰る底の人を覰破す。
text.uk: Майстер підняв монету. «Вона стара, — мовив він. — Та завжди нова. Кожної миті вона народжується.»

author: Tosotsu
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 47 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
A Zen pupil asked Kembo: "All Buddhas of the ten parts of the universe enter the one road of Nirvana. Where does that road begin?"

Kembo, raising his walking stick and drawing the figure one in the air, said: "Here it is."

This pupil went to Ummon and asked the same question. Ummon, who happened to have a fan in his hand, said: "This fan will reach to the thirty-third heaven and hit the nose of the presiding deity there. It is like the Dragon Carp of the Eastern Sea tipping over the rain-cloud with his tail."
text.fr:
Sekitô demanda :
Comment monter encore lorsqu’on est arrivé tout en haut d’un mât de cent pieds ?

Un maître zen dit :

Celui qui s’est assis tout en haut d’un mât de cent pieds a atteint une certaine hauteur… mais il n’est pas encore libre ! Il doit encore continuer à monter pour apparaître de tout son corps dans les dix régions du monde.
text.ja: 乾峰和尚、因みに僧問う、「十方薄伽梵、一路涅槃門。未審し路頭甚麼の處にか在る。」峰、拄杖を拈起して劃一劃して云く、「者裏に在り。」後に僧、雲門に請益す。門、扇子を拈起して云く、「扇子𨁝跳して三十三天に上り、帝釋の鼻孔を築著す。東海の鯉魚、打つこと一棒すれば、雨盆を傾くに似たり。」 無門曰く、「一人は深深たる海底に向って行いて、簸土揚塵し、一人は高高たる山頂に立って、白浪滔天す。把定放行、各一隻手を出して宗乘を扶豎す。大いに兩箇の馳子相撞著するに似たり。世上應に直底の人無かるべし。正眼に觀來れば、二大老惣に未だ路頭を識らざる在。」 頌に曰く、 未だ歩を擧せざる時、先づ已に到る。未だ舌を動ぜざる時、先づ説き了る。 直饒い著著機先に在るも、更に須らく向上の竅有ることをしるべし。
text.uk: Монах гукнув у долину. Відлуння повернулося. «Це не вчення, — мовив майстер. — Вчення ось яке: до того, як ти гукнеш, який звук?»

author: Ummon
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 48 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

text.en:
Amban, a layman Zen student, said: "Mu-mon has just published forty-eight koans and called the book Gateless Gate. He criticizes the old patriarchs' words and actions. I think he is very mischievous. He is like an old doughnut seller trying to catch a passerby to force his doughnuts down his mouth. The customer can neither swallow nor spit out the doughnuts, and this causes suffering. Mu-mon has annoyed everyone enough, so I think I shall add one more as a bargain. I wonder if he himself can eat this bargain. If he can, and digest it well, it will be fine, but if not, we will have to put it back into the frying pan with his forty-eight also and cook them again. Mu-mon, you eat first, before someone else does:

"Buddha, according to a sutra, once said: 'Stop, stop. Do not speak. The ultimate truth is not even to think.'"

 

Amban's comment: Where did that so-called teaching come from? How is it that one could not even think it? Suppose someone spoke about it then what became of it? Buddha himself was a great chatterbox and in this sutra spoke contrarily. Because of this, persons like Mu-mon appear afterwards in China and make useless doughnuts, annoying people. What shall we do after all? I will show you.

Then Amban put his palms together, folded  his hands, and said: "Stop, stop. Do not speak. The ultimate truth is not even to think. And now I will make a little circle on the sutra with my finger and add that five thousand other sutras and Vimalakirti's gateless gate all are here!"

If anyone tells you fire is light,
 Pay no attention.
 When two thieves meet they need no introduction:
 They recognize each other without question.
text.fr:
Tosotsu érigea trois barrières que les moines devraient franchir.

La première barrière est l’étude du zen. Le but de l’étude du zen est de connaître ta vraie nature. Quelle est ta vraie nature ?

La première barrière franchie, la seconde permet de se libérer de la vie et de la mort. Quand s’éteint la lumière de tes yeux, devenant un cadavre, peux-tu te libérer de la vie et de la mort ?

La seconde barrière franchie, la troisième te permet de savoir où tu es. Ton corps étant maintenant séparé en quatre éléments, où es tu ?
text.uk: Майстер мовив: «Дощ падає на всіх однаково. Просвітлені й непросвітлені — всі мокнуть.»

author: Buddha
source: The Gateless Gate (Mumonkan), Case 49 — Mumon Ekai, 1228 — transcribed by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps, 1934 (public domain)

title.en: Finding a Diamond on a Muddy Road
title.fr: La canne de Kembô et l’éventail d’Ummon

text.en: Gudo was the emperor's teacher of Zen. Nevertheless, he used to travel alone as a wandering pilgrim. When he was at the seaside in Edo, some distance from the inn where he was staying, he noticed a tea shop. A girl was working there. "I must buy some tea," thought Gudo, and he called to the girl to bring him a cup. "I'll bring it to you," said the girl, and she brought him a cup of tea. When Gudo held out his hand for the cup, she suddenly poured the tea over his hand. The hot water burned his hand and he nearly dropped the cup. The girl laughed. Startled and angry, Gudo looked at her. "You look like a Zen man," said the girl, "but you don't seem to understand how a person like me fools you. Tell me, now, what is the Buddha?" Gudo tried to answer, but could not. The girl laughed again and went into the shop. Gudo was humiliated. He felt he could not remain in that region. He went to a master and became a serious student at last. After many years he returned home, realizing that he had found a diamond on a muddy road.
text.fr:
Un moine demanda à Kembô :
Tous les bouddhas des dix régions de l’univers avancent sur le chemin unique du nirvâna. Mais où commence ce chemin ?

Kembô leva sa canne et dessina dans l’air l’idéogramme du chiffre UN, disant :

Le voici.

Puis le moine posa la même question à Ummon. Ummon, qui tenait un éventail à la main, dit :

Cet éventail ira jusqu’au trente-troisième ciel et là il frappera le nez de la déité qui y règne. De même le Dragon de la Mer de l’Est perce le nuage chargé de pluie avec sa queue.
text.uk:
Монах спитав: «З чого почати?»
Майстер мовив: «Там, де ти стоїш.»

author: Gudo
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: Zen Master Hakuin was praised by his neighbours as one living a pure life. A beautiful Japanese girl whose parents owned a food store lived near him. Suddenly, without any warning, her parents discovered she was with child. The parents were angry. The girl would not confess who the man was, but after much harassment at last named Hakuin. In great anger the parents went to the master. "Is that so?" was all he would say. After the child was born it was brought to Hakuin. He had lost his reputation, but did not seem to mind. He took very good care of the child. He obtained milk from his neighbours and everything else the little one needed. A year later the girl could stand it no longer. She told her parents the truth — the real father was a young man who worked in the fish market. The parents of the girl at once went to Hakuin, asked his forgiveness, and told him they wanted the child back. Hakuin willingly returned the child. "Is that so?" was all he said.
text.uk: Майстер підняв руку й показав на місяць. «Дивись на місяць, а не на мою руку», — мовив він.

author: Hakuin
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: The Zen master Ho-Shin was about to die. "Is there any last poem?" asked his students. "I have no poem to write," said Ho-Shin. "I only have a few words: Do not kill. Do not steal. Do not be lustful. Do not lie. Do not take wine." "But master," said one student, "anyone can keep those precepts. What is the special teaching of Zen?" "I have no wish to deceive anyone," replied Ho-Shin. "I just keep the precepts. That is the fundamental teaching of all Buddhas and patriarchs. This is indeed the Zen teaching." "Is that all? That is too simple," said the student. "The truth is not complicated," replied Ho-Shin, and passed away.
text.uk:
Монах спитав: «Яке вчення предків?»
Майстер мовив: «Піди до їхньої могили. Спитай у них сам.»

author: Ho-Shin
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: Shun-Kai was the wife of a merchant. She was beautiful, but proud and willful. When her husband died, her relatives tried to persuade her to remarry, but she refused. She intended to become a nun and study Zen. She went to a Zen master and asked him to ordain her. The master looked at her. "You are too beautiful to become a nun," he said. "You will only bring trouble to the monastery." Shun-Kai went home. That night she heated a pot of oil, and when it was boiling she threw it over her face. In the morning she went back to the master. "Now will you ordain me?" she asked. The master looked at her scarred face. "What determination!" he said. "I will ordain you." After her ordination Shun-Kai became a devoted nun. She attained enlightenment and wrote many beautiful poems about the moon.
text.uk: Майстер мовив: «Гірська брама без замка. Та не кожен може ввійти.»

author: Shun-Kai
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: Anyone who has visited China knows that the Chinese people are always smiling. They smile at you when you meet them on the road. They smile at you in the teahouse. They smile at you on the bus. This is not because they have anything special to be happy about. They smile because they have discovered the secret of happiness. The secret is this: Do not expect anything from anyone. Expect nothing, and you will never be disappointed. When you stop expecting, you begin to live in the present moment. And the present moment is the only moment there is. That is why the Chinese are happy.
text.uk: Монах спитав: «У тисячорукого бодгісаттви — тисяча очей. Яке око бачить справжню природу?»

author: Chinese saying
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: In Tokyo in the Meiji era there lived two prominent teachers of opposite characteristics. One was Unsho, an instructor in Shingon. He kept Buddha's precepts scrupulously. He never drank intoxicants, nor did he eat after eleven o'clock in the morning. The other was Tanzan, a professor of philosophy at the Imperial University. He never observed the precepts. When he ate he ate without restraint, and when he slept he slept without restraint. Unsho was considered a saint by the people. One day Unsho visited Tanzan, who was drinking wine, not even a drop of which is supposed to touch a Buddhist's tongue. "Hello, brother," Tanzan greeted him. "Won't you have a drink?" "I never drink!" exclaimed Unsho solemnly. "One who does not drink is not even human," said Tanzan. "Do you mean to say I am not human just because I do not drink intoxicants?" Unsho exclaimed in anger. "Then if I am not human, what am I?" "A Buddha," answered Tanzan.
text.uk:
Монах спитав човняра: «Що таке дзен?»
Човняр мовчки гре6. «Оце дзен», — мовив він.

author: Tanzan
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: Sho-Un became a teacher of Zen. When he was still a student, his mother used to urge him to study harder. She was a very strict mother who wanted him to become a great Zen master. One day Sho-Un was visiting a distant temple. His mother, who was old and ill, wrote him a letter: "I am very ill. Come home at once." When Sho-Un received the letter he did not go home. Instead he wrote back: "I am sorry I cannot come. I am at a very important stage in my training. If I come home now I will lose all my progress. Please understand." When his mother received this letter, she became very angry. She wrote back: "You are a selfish and unfilial son. If you do not come home I will die cursing you." Still Sho-Un did not go home. He continued his Zen training. When at last he attained enlightenment, he returned home. His mother was still alive. She greeted him with tears and said: "Now I know you are a true Zen master. Forgive my anger. I was a foolish old woman."
text.uk: Майстер мовив: «Зимова слива цвіте до того, як розтане сніг. Їй не потрібен дозвіл.»

author: Sho-Un
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A university student visited a Zen master and asked: "Have you ever read the Bible?" "No," answered the master, "tell me about it." The student opened the Bible and read from the Sermon on the Mount: "And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin: And yet I say unto you, that even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these." The Zen master listened quietly. "Excellent!" he exclaimed when the student had finished. "These words are not far from Buddhahood. Whoever uttered them is an enlightened being."
text.uk: Майстер мовив: «Сім квіток розквітають на одній гілці. Кожна різна. Кожна досконала.»

author: University student
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A Zen master named Gettan lived in the northern part of Japan. A young student came to him and asked: "Will you teach me Zen?" "I will," said Gettan, "if you can tell me what Zen is." The student was silent. "Think it over," said Gettan, "and come back when you know." The student went away and thought. He returned the next day. "Zen is the teaching of the Buddha," he said. "That is not it," said Gettan. The student went away again and thought some more. He came back a week later. "Zen is emptiness," he said. "That is not it either," said Gettan. The student went away discouraged. He returned many times with different answers but each time Gettan said no. Finally the student gave up. "Master," he said, "I have no answer. I am a fool." "Now you are ready to learn," said Gettan. "When you know nothing, you can learn everything. I will teach you Zen."
text.uk:
Монах підняв гладенький річковий камінь. «Як він став таким гладеньким?» — спитав він.
Майстер мовив: «Тому що лежав у річці.»

author: Gettan
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: Jiun, a Shingon master, was the son of a Buddhist priest. When his mother was about to die, she asked him: "Will you promise me something?" "Anything, mother," said Jiun. "I want you to promise me that you will never become a Zen master," she said. "Why not?" asked Jiun. "Because I have seen too many Zen masters," she said. "They are proud and arrogant. They think they have special knowledge. They look down on ordinary people. Promise me you will be humble." Jiun promised. He became a great Shingon master. He never sat in the Zen meditation posture. He never used Zen words. But he was a Zen master just the same. When anyone asked him about Zen he would say: "I am not a Zen master. I know nothing about Zen." And he would bow and walk away.
text.uk: Майстер мовив: «Коли входиш у браму храму, залиш усе позаду. Навіть думку про те, що залишаєш.»

author: Jiun
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: Mokusen Hiki was living in a temple in the province of Tamba. One of his followers complained of the stinginess of his wife. Mokusen visited the wife and showed her his clenched fist. "What do you mean by that?" asked the surprised woman. "Suppose my fist were always like that," said Mokusen. "What would you call it?" "Deformed," replied the woman. Then he opened his hand flat in her face and asked: "Suppose it were always like that. What then?" "Another kind of deformity," said the wife. "If you understand that much," said Mokusen, "you are a good wife." He left. After his meal Mokusen returned. "I have a poem for you," he said. "Open your hand and give. Close your hand and keep. Both are deformities. The sage gives and keeps. Neither hand nor mind is tight." And he smiled.
text.uk: Майстер мовив: «Кадильниця тримає попіл. Вона не тримає дим.»

author: Mokusen Hiki
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: Gi-Sho was a nun who studied Zen with Bankei. She attained enlightenment after many years of practice. When Bankei confirmed her realization, he said: 'Now you understand. You must go out and teach others.' Gi-Sho shook her head. 'I don't want to teach,' she said. 'I just want to meditate in peace.' Bankei laughed. 'You think Zen is just sitting?' he said. 'Zen is life. Every moment is Zen. Every action is Zen. Go and work in the world.' Gi-Sho understood. She went to a poor village and started a school for girls. She taught them to read and write. She taught them to meditate. She lived there for many years, helping the poor. When she died the whole village mourned.
text.uk:
Монах спитав: «Яке вчення старої сосни?»
Майстер мовив: «Вона стоїть тисячу років і не мовить ані слова.»

author: Gi-Sho
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A young monk asked his teacher: 'Master, I had a dream last night. In the dream I was a butterfly. I flew from flower to flower. I was happy. But when I woke up I was a monk again. Which is real - the monk or the butterfly?' The master laughed. 'When you dream,' he said, 'you are the butterfly. When you wake, you are the monk. Both are real and neither is real. The truth is beyond both.' The monk was puzzled. 'But what is the truth?' he asked. The master said: 'The truth is that you are asking questions while I am trying to sleep. Good night.' And he closed his eyes.
text.uk: Майстер провів чайну церемонію. Він налив воду, збив чай і подав. Коли закінчив, мовив: «Оце і все.»

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A monk asked Joshu: 'What is Zen?' Joshu said: 'Have you eaten your rice?' 'Yes,' said the monk. 'Then wash your bowl.' At that moment the monk was enlightened. Later another monk asked Joshu: 'What is the meaning of Bodhidharma's coming from the West?' Joshu said: 'The oak tree in the garden.' The monk was puzzled. A third monk asked: 'Does a dog have Buddha-nature?' Joshu said: 'Mu!' This is the most famous koan in all of Zen. Joshu's Zen is simple and direct. It points to the truth of everyday life.
text.uk: Три мудрості — знати себе, забути себе, бути собою. Вони не три.

author: Joshu
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: Tosui was a Zen master who lived as a beggar. He wandered from village to village with only a bowl. He never preached. He never taught. He just begged for food and slept in the fields. One day a wealthy merchant recognized him. 'Master Tosui!' he exclaimed. 'Why do you live like this? You are a great Zen teacher. You could have a temple. You could have disciples.' Tosui held out his bowl. 'I have everything I need,' he said. 'I have food when I am hungry. I have a place to sleep when I am tired. I have the sky for my roof and the earth for my bed. What more could I want?' The merchant was silent. 'You are richer than I am,' he said at last. 'I own many things but I am never satisfied. You own nothing and you are content.' Tosui smiled and walked on.
text.uk:
Майстер підняв перо. «Що легше за це?» — спитав він.
«Ніщо», — відповів монах.
«То чому ти носиш так багато?»

author: Tosui
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

title.en: How Grass and Trees Become Enlightened

text.en: A monk asked his master: 'Do grass and trees also attain enlightenment?' The master said: 'If you say they do, you are wrong. If you say they do not, you are also wrong.' The monk was puzzled. 'What should I say then?' he asked. The master replied: 'Just ask the grass and trees themselves.' The monk went outside and asked a pine tree: 'Do you attain enlightenment?' The pine tree did not answer. The monk returned to the master. 'The pine tree did not answer me,' he said. 'Did you expect it to speak?' asked the master. 'The pine tree has been enlightened from the beginning. It does not need to speak. It does not need to attain anything. It just stands there, being a pine tree. That is its enlightenment.'
text.uk: Майстер мовив: «Є двері без завіс. Є замок без ключа. Як ти ввійдеш?»

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A Zen master was painting a picture of a bamboo grove. He worked on it for many days. When he finished, he showed it to his students. 'What do you think?' he asked. 'It is beautiful,' they said, 'but the proportions seem wrong. The bamboo is too tall and the leaves are too small.' The master laughed. 'You are looking at it from the outside,' he said. 'If you want to see the true proportions, you must become the bamboo.' He took a brush and painted another picture. This time the bamboo was even taller and the leaves even smaller. 'Now,' said the master, 'this is accurate proportion. When you become the bamboo, you see it as it really is.'
text.uk: Брама хитається на завісі. Завіса не рухається. Брама приходить і йде. Завіса лишається.

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A young monk complained to his master: 'The miso soup is sour today.' The master said nothing. The next day the monk complained again: 'The miso soup is still sour.' Still the master said nothing. The third day the monk said: 'Master, the miso has been sour for three days. Should we throw it away?' The master finally spoke: 'The miso is not sour. Your mind is sour. When your mind is sour, everything tastes sour. When your mind is sweet, everything tastes sweet.' The monk felt ashamed. He stopped complaining. From then on, he tried to keep his mind sweet.
text.uk:
Монах спитав: «Яке вчення?»
Майстер мовив: «В'ялена риба. Вона не може повернутися у воду.»

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A student came to his master and said: 'I have been practicing Zen for five years and I have made no progress. I feel like giving up.' The master said: 'Have you ever seen a candle that has burned all night? In the morning, just before dawn, the flame flickers. It seems as if it will go out. But if you keep the wick trimmed, if you keep the wax fresh, the candle will burn until the sun rises. Your practice is like that. The darkest hour is just before dawn. Don't give up now. Your light may flicker, but it will not go out. Keep going. The dawn is near.' The student took heart and continued his practice. Soon after, he attained enlightenment.
text.uk: Храмовий барабан розбився. Майстер мовив: «Тепер він звучить досконало.»

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A Zen master was dying. His students gathered around him. 'Master,' they said, 'leave us your last teaching.' The master opened his eyes. 'I have nothing to leave you,' he said. 'I have taught you everything I know. Now you must walk your own path.' 'But master,' they insisted, 'at least leave us a poem.' The master smiled weakly. 'My whole life has been my poem,' he said. 'Every breath, every step, every word. If you have understood my life, you have my last teaching. If you have not, no poem will help you.' He closed his eyes. A moment later he opened them again. 'Oh, one more thing,' he said. 'Don't forget to water the garden.' Then he died.
text.uk: Майстер мовив: «Павук плете павутиння. Він не планує. Він не думає. Він просто плете.»

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

title.en: The Tea Master and the Assassin

text.en: A tea master was challenged by a samurai who wanted to kill him. The tea master was not a fighter. He was afraid. He went to a Zen master and asked for advice. The Zen master said: 'You are a tea master. When you prepare tea, you are fully present. Your mind is calm. Your movements are precise. Face the samurai with the same mind you have when you make tea.' The tea master understood. He went to meet the samurai. He bowed. He took out his tea utensils. He began to prepare tea with complete concentration. His movements were graceful and precise. The samurai watched in amazement. He had never seen such presence of mind. When the tea master finished, he offered the samurai a cup. The samurai took it and drank. Then he bowed deeply and left. He could not kill a man with such a calm and centered mind.
text.uk: Осінній листок падає. Чи опирається він? Чи скаржиться? Він просто падає.

author: Tea master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A young monk asked his master: 'Master, which is the true path to enlightenment? Should I meditate in the mountains? Should I study the sutras? Should I serve the poor?' The master said: 'The true path is right where you are.' 'But I don't understand,' said the monk. 'I am here in the monastery. Is this the true path?' 'The true path,' said the master, 'is washing your bowl after eating. It is sweeping the floor. It is greeting your brothers. It is sitting in meditation. It is all of these and none of these. The true path is not a destination. It is the way you walk. Walk with full attention, and every step is the true path.'
text.uk: Два монахи дивилися, як майорить прапор. Один сказав, що вітер рухається. Другий сказав, що прапор рухається. Майстер мовив: «Ваші розуми рухаються.»

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A soldier came to Hakuin and asked: 'Master, is there really a paradise and a hell?' Hakuin looked at the soldier with contempt. 'Who are you?' he asked. 'I am a samurai,' the soldier replied proudly. 'You, a samurai?' Hakuin laughed. 'You look more like a beggar to me.' The soldier became angry. He drew his sword. Hakuin said calmly: 'Here open the gates of hell.' The soldier understood. He sheathed his sword and bowed. 'And here,' said Hakuin, 'open the gates of paradise.'
text.uk: Монах гукнув у долину. Відлуння повернулося. «Це не вчення, — мовив майстер. — Вчення — це тиша між криком і відлунням.»

author: Hakuin
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A merchant came to a Zen master and said: 'Someone has been stealing from my shop. I suspect a monk from the nearby temple. What should I do?' The master said: 'Arrest the stone Buddha in the garden.' 'Why?' asked the merchant. 'Because the stone Buddha sees everything,' said the master. 'If you arrest the Buddha, he will tell you who stole.' The merchant arrested the stone Buddha and brought it to the magistrate. The magistrate laughed. 'Why have you brought a stone Buddha to court?' 'Because he saw the thief,' said the merchant. The magistrate understood. He said: 'The stone Buddha is innocent. The true thief is your own suspicion. Go home and forgive whoever stole from you.' The merchant went home. The next day, the stolen goods were returned anonymously.
text.uk: Майстер ішов бамбуковим гаєм. Вітер шелестів листям. «Слухай, — мовив він. — Бамбук проповідує.»

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A Zen master was asked about war and peace. He said: 'The greatest battle is not fought with swords. It is fought in the heart. The enemy is not another person. The enemy is your own ignorance, your own anger, your own greed. Conquer these, and you have conquered all enemies. True warriors are not those who kill others. True warriors are those who kill their own delusions. They are soldiers of humanity, fighting the war against suffering.' The student asked: 'But what about those who wage real war?' The master replied: 'They have not yet learned to fight the only battle that matters. Pity them, and teach them peace.'
text.uk:
Біля храму жила стара жінка. Вона ніколи не практикувала дзен. Одного дня майстер спитав її: «Яка твоя практика?»
Вона відповіла: «Я підмітаю підлогу.»

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A young man came to a Zen master and said: 'I am very unhappy. Everything goes wrong in my life. Nothing ever works out for me. I think I am cursed.' The master said: 'Give me your hand.' The young man held out his hand. The master studied his palm. 'I see,' said the master. 'Your lifeline shows you will live to be eighty. Your fortune line shows you will be rich. Your love line shows you will have a happy marriage. But none of this matters.' 'Why not?' asked the young man. 'Because,' said the master, 'the lines in your hand change with every thought, every action, every moment. You are not in the hands of destiny. Destiny is in your hands.'
text.uk: Лотос росте в багнюці. Та цвіте чистим і білим. Багнюка — не його ворог.

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A Zen master was asked how many disciples he had. 'Ten,' he replied. 'But master,' said the student, 'I see only five in the meditation hall.' 'Some of my disciples are not in the hall,' said the master. 'One is a fisherman. One is a farmer. One is a merchant. One is a mother. One is a child.' The student was confused. 'How can they be your disciples if they do not meditate?' he asked. 'They meditate while fishing,' said the master. 'They meditate while farming. They meditate while selling. They meditate while raising children. They meditate while playing. Zen is not only in the meditation hall. It is everywhere. My real disciples are those who bring Zen into everyday life.'
text.uk: Мох росте на кам'яній стежці. Крок за кроком, стежка веде в нікуди. Та кожен крок прибуває.

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A monk said to his master: 'I want to become a better person. I want to reform myself. What should I do?' The master asked: 'What do you think is wrong with you?' The monk listed his faults: anger, laziness, greed, pride. The master nodded. 'These are not your faults,' he said. 'These are your teachers. Each one has something to teach you. Instead of fighting them, learn from them.' 'But how?' asked the monk. 'When anger arises,' said the master, 'do not suppress it. Observe it. Where does it come from? Where does it go? When you understand anger, you are free from anger. This is true reformation - not to change yourself, but to understand yourself.'
text.uk: Полуденний дзвін дзвенить. Монахи збираються. «До того, як дзвін пролунав, — спитав майстер, — де ви були?»

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A student was meditating when he smelled incense. He opened his eyes and saw his master burning incense. 'Master,' said the student, 'the incense is distracting me. I cannot meditate.' The master took the incense burner and placed it in front of the student. 'Now meditate on the incense,' he said. 'Do not resist it. Become one with it.' The student closed his eyes. He breathed in the scent. He became the scent. He forgot himself. When he opened his eyes, an hour had passed. 'Now you understand,' said the master. 'Zen is not about avoiding distractions. It is about becoming one with everything, including distractions.'
text.uk: Досконалий шлях — без труднощів. Він лише уникає обрання та відкидання. Коли вподобання й невподобання забуті — все стає ясним.

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A master said: 'There are three kinds of disciples. The first kind hears the teaching and immediately understands. The second kind hears the teaching and thinks about it. The third kind hears the teaching and rejects it. All three reach the same destination. It just takes different amounts of effort.' A student asked: 'Which kind am I, master?' The master said: 'The kind that asks questions instead of finding out for himself.'
text.uk: Безмежне небо не має меж. Птахи летять крізь нього й не лишають сліду. Нехай твій розум буде, як небо.

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A young monk was trying to light a fire. He struck match after match but the wood would not catch. He became frustrated. He struck harder. The matches broke. He threw down the box in anger. The master, who had been watching, picked up a fire poker. He stirred the ashes gently. A small ember glowed beneath the surface. He placed a piece of kindling on it and blew softly. A flame appeared. 'Sometimes,' said the master, 'the fire is already there. You just need to uncover it. Zen is not about creating something new. It is about uncovering what is already there.'
text.uk: Майстер мовив: «Життя — немов крапля роси на травинці. За мить її нема. Та в ту мить у ній відбивається цілий світ.»

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A monk said: 'Master, I have given up everything. I own nothing. I am free.' The master pointed to the monk's robe. 'You are attached to that robe,' he said. The monk took off his robe. 'Now I have nothing,' he said. 'You are attached to having nothing,' said the master. The monk was silent. 'Non-attachment,' said the master, 'is not about having nothing. It is about being free even when you have everything. It is about holding things lightly, with open hands. A man who clings to poverty is as attached as a man who clings to wealth.'
text.uk: Старий храм стоїть порожній. Статуя Будди зникла. Вівтар голий. «Тепер це справжній храм», — мовив майстер.

author: Zen master
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A student asked: 'Master, what is the Buddha's Zen?' The master held up a flower. 'Is that all?' asked the student. The master put the flower down. 'No,' he said. 'The flower is just a flower. The Buddha's Zen is not in the flower. It is in the seeing. When you see the flower without any thought, without any judgment, without any name - that is the Buddha's Zen. The flower is just a pointer. The real teaching is wordless.' The student looked at the flower. He tried to see without thinking. After a long silence, he smiled. 'I see,' he said. 'What do you see?' asked the master. 'Just a flower,' said the student.
text.uk: Майстер мовив: «Відчини садову браму. Впусти вітер. Впусти місячне сяйво. Не тримай нічого назовні.»

author: Buddha Shakyamuni
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: The Buddhist nun, known as Ryo-Nen, was born in 1797. She was a granddaughter of the famous Japanese warrior, Shingen. Her poetical genius and alluring beauty were such that at seventeen she was serving the Empress as one of the ladies of the Court. Even at such a youthful age fame awaited her. The beloved Empress died suddenly and Ryo-Nen's hopeful dreams vanished. She became acutely aware of the impermanency of life in this world. It was then that she desired to study Zen. Her relatives, however, disagreeing, practically forced her into marriage. With a promise that she might become a nun after she had borne three children, Ryo-Nen assented. Before she was twenty-five she had accomplished this condition. Then her husband and relatives could no longer dissuade her from her desire. She shaved her head, took the name of Ryo-Nen which means to realize clearly and started on her pilgrimage. She came to the city of Edo and asked Tetsu-Gyu to accept her as a disciple. At one glance the master rejected her because she was too beautiful. Ryo-Nen then went to another master, Haku-Wo. Haku-Wo refused her for the same reason, saying that her beauty would only make trouble. Ryo-Nen obtained a hot iron and placed it against her face. In a few moments her beauty had vanished forever. Haku-Wo then accepted her as a disciple. When Ryo-Nen was about to pass from this world, she wrote a poem: 'Sixty-six times have these eyes beheld the changing scene of Autumn. I have said enough about moonlight. Ask no more. Only listen to the voice of pines and cedars when no wind stirs.'
text.uk: Три скарби — це Будда, дгарма і санґга. Де вони? У твоєму власному розумі.

author: Ryo-Nen
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: Ka-San was asked to officiate at the funeral of a provincial lord. He had never met lords and nobles before, so he was nervous. When the ceremony started, Ka-San sweat. Afterwards when he had returned he gathered his pupils together. Ka-San confessed that he was not yet qualified to be a teacher, for he lacked the sameness of bearing in the world of fame that he possessed in the secluded temple. Then Ka-San resigned and became the pupil of another master. Eight years later he returned to his former pupils, enlightened.
text.uk: Черепаха ховається в панцир. Вона думає, що це безпечно. Та панцир — просто ще одне місце, де ховатися.

author: Ka-San
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: To-Sui was the Zen master who left the formalism of temples to live under a bridge with beggars. When he was getting very old, a friend helped him to earn his living without begging. He showed To-Sui how to collect rice and manufacture vinegar from it, and To-Sui did this until he passed away. While To-Sui was making vinegar, one of the beggars gave him a picture of the Buddha. To-Sui hung it on the wall of his hut and put a sign beside it. It read: 'Mr. Amida Buddha: This little room is quite narrow. I can let you remain as a transient. But do not think I am asking you to help me to be reborn in your paradise.'
text.uk: Майстер заграв на бамбуковій флейті. Коли закінчив, мовив: «Флейта порожня. Без порожнечі не було б музики.»

author: To-Sui
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: Tanzan wrote sixty postcards on the last day of his life. He asked a messenger to mail them. Then he passed away. The cards read: 'I am departing from this world. This is my last announcement. Tanzan. July 27, 1892.'
text.uk: Лампада горить усю ніч. Вона дає світло всім, хто приходить. Вона не просить нічого взамін.

author: Tanzan
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

title.en: What Are You Doing! What Are You Saying!

text.en: A Zen master named Kyogen said: 'Zen is like a man hanging in a tree by his teeth over a precipice. His hands grasp no branch, his feet rest on no limb, and under the tree another person asks him: Why did Bodhidharma come to China from India? If the man in the tree does not answer, he fails, and if he does answer, he falls and loses his life. Now what shall he do?' A student raised his hand and said: 'Master, may I ask a question?' Kyogen said: 'Go ahead.' The student said: 'What would you have done?' Kyogen laughed. 'I would not have climbed the tree in the first place,' he said.
text.uk: У полудень сонце світить просто згори. Немає тіні. Це розум просвітлення.

author: Kyogen
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

text.en: A Zen student came to Bankei and said: 'Master, I have an ungovernable temper. How can I cure it?' 'You have something very strange,' said Bankei. 'Let me see what you have.' 'Just now I cannot show it to you,' replied the student. 'When can you show it to me?' asked Bankei. 'It arises unexpectedly,' replied the student. 'Then,' concluded Bankei, 'it must not be your own true nature. If it were, you could show it to me at any time. When you were born you did not have it, and your parents did not give it to you. Think that over.'
text.uk: Після довгої подорожі ти повертаєшся додому. Двері відчинені. Вогонь горить. Нічого не змінилося. Все інакше.

author: Bankei
source: 101 Zen Stories (1919), compiled by Nyogen Senzaki & Paul Reps

title.en: The World-Honored One Ascends the Rostrum

text.en:
Even if you close the gates and stay asleep, you can guide those with the highest aspiration.  You dare look to and fro, and bend and stretch your body – 
only for the sake of those with the mediocre and low aspiration.  
How could you bear sitting on the curved wooden chair and sport with your devil’s eyes?  
If there is anyone nearby who does not agree, step forward.  
Never would I consider him a queer fellow.

One day, the World-Honored One ascended to the rostrum.  Manjusri struck the table with the gavel and said, “Contemplate clearly the Dharma of the Dharma-King!  The Dharma of the Dharma-King is like this!”  Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from the rostrum.

The true wind of supremacy – do you see it or not?
Mother Creation moves incessantly her loom and shuttle,
Weaving the ancient brocade, embracing all forms of spring.
How could you stop the Prince of East from leaking them?
text.uk:
Монах спитав Енкьо: «У чому сенс приходу Бодгідгарми із Заходу?»
Енкьо мовив: «Вежа на вершині гори.»
Монах спитав: «Я не розумію.»
Енкьо мовив: «Шкода стовпа у домі міністра.»

author: Wanshi Shogaku (Hongzhi Zhengjue) / Wansong Xingxiu
source: Book of Equanimity / Shoyo-roku (1224), transl. Sanbo Kyodan Society

text.en:
Benka presented the jewel three times, yet he did not escape punishment1.  
When a luminous jewel is thrown to anyone in the darkness, most probably they would get ready to draw their sword.  
For an impromptu guest there is no impromptu host.  
What is only expediently appropriate, is never truly appropriate.  
If you cannot make avail of the rare and unusual treasure, 
I will present to you the head of a dead cat.  Look!

Emperor Bu of Ryô asked Great Master Bodhidharma, “What is the highest meaning of the holy reality?”  Bodhidharma replied, “Vast and void, no holiness.”  The emperor said, “Who are you in front of me?”  Bodhidharma said, “I don't know.”  The emperor did not match him.  Finally, Bodhidharma crossed the Yangtze River and came to the Shôrin Temple.  There he sat for nine years, facing the wall.

Vast and void, no holiness – 
The practitioner comes, missing the mark by far.
One gains, when one swings one’s axe without hurting the nose,
One loses, when one drops the pot without turning back.
In solitude he sits coolly in the Temple Shôrin,
In silence he manifests the absolute command.
In the clean pure autumn the moon rotates its frosty wheel,
In the pale Milky Way the Dipper’s handle hangs low in the dark.
The robe and bowl have been handed down to the descendents in succession,
Bringing medicine and disease for humans and heavenly beings.
text.uk: Монах спитав Кемпі: «У чому сенс приходу Бодгідгарми із Заходу?»\nКемпі мовив: «Кипарис у саду.»

author: Wanshi Shogaku (Hongzhi Zhengjue) / Wansong Xingxiu
source: Book of Equanimity / Shoyo-roku (1224), transl. Sanbo Kyodan Society

title.en: The Indian King Invites the Patriarch

text.en:
The activity prier to the beginning of kalpas, before any signs ever emerge – 
A blind turtle goes into the fire.
The one phrase transmitted outside the scriptures – 
Flowers bloom upon the beaks of a stone mill.
Just tell me, do you have the capacity to accept, maintain, read and recite sutras or not?

A king of Eastern India invited the twenty-seventh patriarch, Prajna Tara, for a meal.  The king asked, “Why don't you recite sutras?”  The patriarch said, “The poor way2 does not stay in the world of subject when breathing in, and has nothing to do with the world of objects when breathing out.  I am always reciting the suchness-sutra in millions and millions of volumes.”

A cloud rhinoceros plays with the moon, [with its horns] bearing the radiant light;
A wooden horse romps in spring, unbridled and swift.
Beneath the eyebrows, a pair of blue eyes are cold:
Why should the reading of scriptures pierce through the ox skin?
The clear mind transcends vast kalpas;
The hero’s power smashes the enclosures thick and fast.
The pivot holes of the subtle round disks turn in wondrous activities:
Kanzan has forgotten the path by which he came;
Jittoku leads him back by the hand.
text.uk: Майстер мовив: «Слухай звук порожнечі. Він немов відлуння в пустій долині. Але долина не народжувала відлуння.»

author: Wanshi Shogaku (Hongzhi Zhengjue) / Wansong Xingxiu
source: Book of Equanimity / Shoyo-roku (1224), transl. Sanbo Kyodan Society

title.en: The World-Honored One Points to the Ground

text.en:
Once a speck of dust arises, the whole great earth is embraced in it.  
With a single horse and with a single lance 
You enlarge the territory and widen the boundaries – that is not impossible.  
Who is the person who can be master at any place and embody the principle in any karma?

When the World-Honored One was walking with his assembly, he pointed to the ground with his hand and said, “This place is good for building a temple.”  Indra3 took a stalk of grass and stuck it in the ground and said, “The temple has been built.”  The World-Honored One smiled.

The boundless spring upon a hundred plants –
Taking up whatever comes to hand, he can use it familiarly:
The golden body of sixteen feet, an assemblage of virtues,
Walks casually, hand in hand [with his mates], into the scarlet dusts.
He is able to be master amid all the dusts,
With the guest spontaneously appearing from beyond the world [where preaching is due] 4.
Everywhere life is sufficient according to its portion;
It does not matter whether you are inferior to someone else or not.
text.uk: Монах спитав: «А що ж три світи?»\nМайстер мовив: «Де ти стоїш?»

author: Wanshi Shogaku (Hongzhi Zhengjue) / Wansong Xingxiu
source: Book of Equanimity / Shoyo-roku (1224), transl. Sanbo Kyodan Society

text.en:
Shadai cut off his flesh to feed his parents, 
but he could not be enrolled in the list of filial children.  
Devadatta pushed a mountain to crush the Buddha, 
yet did he ever fear the peals of abrupt thunder?  
Pass through the jungle of thorns, chop down the forest of sandalwood, 
and wait till the year comes to an end.  
As of old, early spring is still chilly.  
Where is the Dharma body of the Buddha at all?

A monk asked Seigen, “What is the essence of Buddha’s Dharma?”  Seigen said, “What is the price of rice in Roryô5?”

The reign of great peace knows no form:
The atmosphere of the rugged old man is superbly pristine,
There are nothing but singing and drinking of the village festival;
How could they be aware of the virtues of Shun and the good will of Gyô6?
text.uk: Майстер Хакуін мовив: «Ти чуєш звук двох долонь, що плескають. А який звук однієї долоні?»

author: Wanshi Shogaku (Hongzhi Zhengjue) / Wansong Xingxiu
source: Book of Equanimity / Shoyo-roku (1224), transl. Sanbo Kyodan Society

text.en:
When you cannot open your mouth, a person without a tongue can speak.  
When you do not lift up your feet, a person without legs can walk.  
If you fall within the range of your opponent’s arrow and die under the phrase, how can you show the status of freedom?  
When the four mountains are about to oppress you, how can you attain thorough liberation?

A monk asked Great Master Ba, “Apart from the four Phrases, beyond one hundred Negations, please tell me directly, Master, the meaning of Bodhidharma's coming from the West.”  Master Ba said, “I am tired today, I can't explain it to you.  Go and ask Chizô.”  The monk asked Chizô about it.  Chizô said, “Why don't you ask our master?”  The monk said, “He told me to ask you.”  Chizô said, “I have a headache today, I can't explain it to you.  Go and ask Brother Kai7.”  The monk asked Brother Kai about it.  Kai said, “I understand nothing about that question.”  The monk told Great Master Ba about it.  Great Master said, “ Chizô's head is white, Kai's head is black.”

Medicine causing illness – the past sages are the mirror of this.
Illness becoming medicine – who can demonstrate this at all?
White head, black head – the children augmenting the esteem of the house.
Speech and non-speech – they are able to cut off the streams.
[Through sitting] they magnificently chop off the roads of the tongue tip.
How laughable – the ancient Awl of Biya8!
text.uk: Монах спитав: «Яке звання має майстер дзен?»\nМайстер мовив: «Жодного.»

author: Wanshi Shogaku (Hongzhi Zhengjue) / Wansong Xingxiu
source: Book of Equanimity / Shoyo-roku (1224), transl. Sanbo Kyodan Society

text.en:
Eyes, ears, nose, tongue – each has its function,
[While] the eyebrows sit [far] above.  
Warriors, farmers, craftspeople, merchants – each has their work to do,
[While] a man of no activity is always at leisure.  
What method does a true master apply to teach the students?

Yakusan had not ascended the rostrum for a long time.  The temple steward said, “All the assembly has been wishing for instruction for a long time.  Please, Master, give your assembly a sermon.”
Yakusan had the bell rung.  The assembly gathered.  Yakusan ascended the rostrum and sat there for a while.  Then he descended and returned to his room.
The temple steward followed him and asked, “You said a while ago that you would give the assembly a sermon.  Why didn't you speak even a word?”  Yakusan said, “For sutras, there are sutra specialists; for sastras9, there are sastra specialists.  Why do you have doubts about this old monk?”

A foolish child endeavors to give the kids “toy money” to stop them from crying;
[Even] the four good horses and the “wind-chasing” steed10 see the shadow of the whip.
[While] the clouds sweep the wide open sky, the crane nests in the moon;
With the cold purity sinking into the bones, he never goes to sleep.
text.uk: Майстер мовив: «Меч розуму пробиває все. Та де його лезо?»

author: Wanshi Shogaku (Hongzhi Zhengjue) / Wansong Xingxiu
source: Book of Equanimity / Shoyo-roku (1224), transl. Sanbo Kyodan Society

text.en:
If you memorize the character for “One” and stick to it in your heart, 
You will swiftly fall into hell like an arrow.  
If you have swallowed one drop of slobber of the fox, 
You can never spit it out for thirty years.  
It is not that the Law in India has been too strict; 
It is just that the karma of the stupid beast has been miserable.  
Has there ever been anyone who has committed such a transgression?

Whenever Master Hyakujô delivered a sermon, an old man was always there listening with the monks.  When they left, he left too.  One day, however, he remained behind.  Hyakujô asked him, “What man are you, standing there?”  The old man replied, “ In the past, in the time of Kashyapa Buddha, I lived on this mountain as a Zen priest.  Once a monk came and asked me, 'Does a perfectly enlightened person fall under the law of cause and effect or not?'  I said to him, 'He does not.”  Because of this answer, I fell into the state of a fox for 500 lives.  Now, I beg you, Master, please say a turning word.”  Hyakujô said, “The law of cause and effect cannot be obscured.”  Upon hearing this, the old man became greatly enlightened.

One foot of water, one fathom of wave.
It was impossible to do anything for five hundred lives.
They have been arguing whether it is “not falling” or “not obscuring,” 
Always being caught up in the pit of entangling vines.
Ha! ha! ha!  Do you understand it or not?
If you are completely detached and at ease, you do not object to my babbling talk.
People sing and dance at the shrine festival, creating spontaneous accord;
While clapping the hands, they chant around in merry unison.
text.uk: Монах спитав: «А що ж десять тисяч речей?»\nМайстер мовив: «Одна річ.»

author: Wanshi Shogaku (Hongzhi Zhengjue) / Wansong Xingxiu
source: Book of Equanimity / Shoyo-roku (1224), transl. Sanbo Kyodan Society

text.uk: Досконалий шлях — без труднощів. Він лише уникає обрання та відкидання.

author: Wanshi Shogaku (Hongzhi Zhengjue) / Wansong Xingxiu
source: Book of Equanimity / Shoyo-roku (1224), transl. Sanbo Kyodan Society

text.en:
Gathering and releasing – the stick is always with him; 
Able to kill and able to give life – the balance remains in his hands.  
Delusive passions, devils and non-Buddhists – he controls them all at his finger tip; 
The great earth, the mountains and rivers – all become his toys.  
Just tell me, what sort of inner dimension is this?

There was an old woman on the way to Taizan.  Whenever a monk asked her how to get to Taizan, she would answer, “Go straight on.”  After the monk had gone a few steps, she would say, “This good and naïve fellow goes off that way, too.”  
Later a monk told Jôshû about this.  Jôshû said, “Wait a bit.  I will go and see through her for you.”  He went and asked the same question.
The next day, Jôshû ascended the rostrum and said, “I have seen through the old woman for you.”

Old in age, he has become a spirit, making no mistakes in transmission;
The old buddha Jôshû succeeded to Nansen.
The old turtle loses its life because of the designs on its back16;
Even the “excellent four horses”17 and the “Wind Chaser”18 are encumbered by the bridle.
The “old woman's Zen” has been seen through:
If you preach it to people, it isn't worth a penny.
text.uk: Коли великий майстер мав померти, його тіло розчинилося в райдузі. Учні спитали: «Куди він пішов?»

author: Wanshi Shogaku (Hongzhi Zhengjue) / Wansong Xingxiu
source: Book of Equanimity / Shoyo-roku (1224), transl. Sanbo Kyodan Society

text.uk: Одна природа, досконала і всюдисуща, протікає крізь усі природи. Одна реальність, усеосяжна, вміщує всі реальності.

author: Wanshi Shogaku (Hongzhi Zhengjue) / Wansong Xingxiu
source: Book of Equanimity / Shoyo-roku (1224), transl. Sanbo Kyodan Society

text.uk: До народження твоїх батьків — яке було твоє справжнє обличчя?

author: Wanshi Shogaku (Hongzhi Zhengjue) / Wansong Xingxiu
source: Book of Equanimity / Shoyo-roku (1224), transl. Sanbo Kyodan Society

text.en:
Totally dedicated to helping others, one does not recognize one's own self.  
One implements the Law to the full, disregarding the fact that almost all people have fled away.  
One must have harsh and decisive means to twist and break the wooden pillow.  
But when one faces death, what then?

When Rinzai was about to die, he entrusted Sanshô with his Dharma and said, “After my passing, do not destroy my treasury of the Eye of the true Dharma23.”  Sanshô said, “How would I dare destroy your treasury of the Eye of the true Dharma?”  Rinzai said, “If someone asks you about it, how will you answer?”  Sanshô instantly shouted, “Kaatzu!”  Rinzai said, “Who knows that my treasury of the Eye of the true Dharma has been destroyed by this blind donkey!”

At midnight, the robe of faith is granted to Ronô24;
The seven hundred monks on Mt Ôbai25 were thrown into an uproar.
A branch of the Eye of true Dharma of Rinzai26 –
The blind donkey destroyed it, which provoked hatred of all people.
Heart to heart they seal each other; 
Ancestor to ancestor they transmit the lamp.
One flattens the seas and mountains, letting the giant birds come out.
The splendid phrase is beyond comparison;
One knows the method to turn things over and let them soar.
text.uk: Майстер мовив: «Віл загубився. Пастух шукає його всюди. Коли вони зустрічаються, віл зникає.»

author: Wanshi Shogaku (Hongzhi Zhengjue) / Wansong Xingxiu
source: Book of Equanimity / Shoyo-roku (1224), transl. Sanbo Kyodan Society

text.uk: Майстер мовив: «Не думай про ущелину. Думай про те, що за ущелиною.»

author: Wanshi Shogaku (Hongzhi Zhengjue) / Wansong Xingxiu
source: Book of Equanimity / Shoyo-roku (1224), transl. Sanbo Kyodan Society

title.en: Kyôzan Thrusts His Hoe into the Ground

text.en:
Knowing before it is spoken – this is called silent speech; 
Manifesting oneself before anything is revealed – it is called a dark activity.
Making gassho in front of the main gate, walking down the hallway
 – it is a spontaneous communication.
Dancing in the inner garden, wagging the head at the back gate – what is this?

Isan asked Kyôzan, “Where have you come from?”  Kyôzan said, “From the rice field.”  Isan said, “How many people are there in the rice field?”  Kyôzan thrust his hoe into the ground and stood with his hands folded on his chest.  Isan said, “There are a great number of people cutting thatch on the South Mountain.”  Kyôzan took up his hoe and left immediately.

The old enlightened one affectionately thinks of his descendants.
Now [the descendant] repents and thus erects a household.
Remember well the saying about South Mountain:
Engrave it on your bones, inscribe it on your skin, 
And return the kindness you all have received.
text.uk: Майстер мовив: «Пустота — це не ніщо. Це все без форми.»

author: Wanshi Shogaku (Hongzhi Zhengjue) / Wansong Xingxiu
source: Book of Equanimity / Shoyo-roku (1224), transl. Sanbo Kyodan Society

text.en:
Pointing to a deer, you make it a horse,
Grabbing some soil, you turn it to gold; 
Creating wind and thunder upon the tongue, 
Hiding a bloody blade between the eyebrows,
You observe defeat and victory while sitting,
You examine death and life while standing.
Just tell me, what samadhi is this?

Mayoku, with his ring-staff in hand, came to Shôkei31.  He circled Shôkei's dais three times, shook the ring-staff and stood there bolt upright.  Shôkei said, “Right, right!”  Mayoku then came to Nansen.  He circled Nansen's dais three times, shook the ring-staff and stood there bolt upright.  Nansen said, “Not right, not right!”  Then, Mayoku said, “Master Shôkei said, 'Right, right!'  Why, Master, do you say, 'Not right, not right!'?”  Nansen said, “With Shôkei it is right, but with you it is not right.  This is nothing but a whirling of the wind.  In the end, it will perish.”

“Right” and “not right” – be clever enough to see the trap.
Seemingly suppressing, seemingly upholding –
Difficult to say, which is the elder brother and which the younger:
This one acknowledged him, simply acting according to the occasion,
That one denied him, performing nothing special.
With one shake of the golden staff, he stood all alone,
Circling around the seat three times, he played with no ulterior thoughts.
But Zen monasteries are agitated, “good” and “bad” are created,
As if they saw ghosts in front of a skull.
text.uk: Майстер Банкей навчав: «Ненароджене — це розум Будди. Воно ніколи не народжувалось і ніколи не помре. Воно присутнє в кожному.»

author: Wanshi Shogaku (Hongzhi Zhengjue) / Wansong Xingxiu
source: Book of Equanimity / Shoyo-roku (1224), transl. Sanbo Kyodan Society

text.uk: Монах спитав: «У чому вчення школи Волячої голови?»\nМайстер мовив: «Віл не знає власної сили.»

author: Wanshi Shogaku (Hongzhi Zhengjue) / Wansong Xingxiu
source: Book of Equanimity / Shoyo-roku (1224), transl. Sanbo Kyodan Society

text.en:
Touch a gourd floating on the water, and it turns; 
Hold a jewel in the sunlight, and its colors show no fixed forms.  
It cannot be attained by the mind of Mu [= there is not], 
Nor can it be known by the mind of U [= there is].  
Even surpassingly great people are turned over in the flow of words.  
Is there anyone who can escape from it?

A monk asked Jôshû, “Does the dog have buddha-nature, or not?”  Jôshû said, “It does [U].”  The monk said, “If it does, why did it creep into that skin bag?”  Jôshû said, “Because it does so knowingly.”
Another monk asked, “Does the dog have buddha-nature, or not?”  Jôshû said, “It does not [Mu]”.  The monk said, “All living beings have buddha-nature35.  Why doesn't the dog have any?”  Jôshû said, “Because its karma-consciousness is in it.”

The dog – buddha-nature – U [= there is]! 
The dog – buddha-nature – Mu [= there is not]!
A straight hook intrinsically seeks a fish who would disregard life36.
[Yet] practicing monks are chasing the air and running after fragrance,
Making noisy and confused excuses.
He [, however,] presents it evenly, throwing the shop completely open;
Don't consider it strange that he wasn't mindful enough at the beginning.
Pointing out the flaw, Rinshôjo took back the jewel;
The emperor of Shin didn't know him37.
text.uk: Монах спитав: «Що таке дзен?»\nМайстер мовив: «П'яний від порожнечі.»

author: Wanshi Shogaku (Hongzhi Zhengjue) / Wansong Xingxiu
source: Book of Equanimity / Shoyo-roku (1224), transl. Sanbo Kyodan Society

text.en:
“I cherish the activities of Shôyô and Shinjô:
All through their lives they pulled out nails and wedges from the people.”38
Why did they sometimes open the door and present a bowl of glue, 
Or dig a pitfall on the road?
Try to examine and see!

A monk asked Unmon. “Not a single thought arises:  is there any fault or not?”  Unmon said, “Mt. Sumeru39.”

Not-a-single-thought-arising – Mt. Sumeru:
The way Shôyô40 presents the Dharma is not stingy at all.
If you can accept it, he gives it to you with both hands;
If you have a doubt, it’s so steep you can never climb it.
The blue ocean is wide, the white clouds are calm;
Do not put even a single hair in there.
A fake cock crow can hardly deceive me;
I will never let you cheat around and pass through the gate41.
text.uk: Майстер мовив: «Десять тисяч доріг ведуть до однієї брами. Та брама не має дверей.»

author: Wanshi Shogaku (Hongzhi Zhengjue) / Wansong Xingxiu
source: Book of Equanimity / Shoyo-roku (1224), transl. Sanbo Kyodan Society

text.en:
The profound speech leading into the ultimate principle despises “three” and tears up “four.”  The great way to the Capital Chôan runs in all directions.  
If you suddenly open up your mouth and preach to the full, or move your legs and take steps, Then you can hang up your meal bowl with the bag and break off your wandering staff.  
Now just tell me, who is like this?

Jizô asked Hôgen, “Where are you going, senior monk42?”  Hôgen said, “I am on pilgrimage43, wandering with the wind.”  Jizô said, “What is pilgrimage?”  Hôgen said, “I don’t know.”  Jizô said, “Non-knowing is most intimate.”  Hôgen suddenly attained great enlightenment.

Now, having practiced to the end, it is just like as it was at the beginning –
Having rid yourself of all intricacies you reach the non-knowing.
Let it be short, or let it be long – you cease pruning and patching;
Follow the high, or follow the low – it levels by itself.
Richness of the family or its scarcity – you use it according to the occasion;
You walk leisurely around in your land, you go where your feet lead you.
That you set out on pilgrimage thirty years ago – 
How clearly it ran counter to the fact of your two eyebrows!
text.uk: Монах спитав: «Що таке брама дракона?»\nМайстер мовив: «Коли короп пливе проти течії і стрибає через водоспад, він стає драконом.»

author: Wanshi Shogaku (Hongzhi Zhengjue) / Wansong Xingxiu
source: Book of Equanimity / Shoyo-roku (1224), transl. Sanbo Kyodan Society

text.en:
Having come out of delusion and enlightenment, and annihilated holy and ordinary – you find there is nothing special.
And yet establishing host and guest and distinguishing noble and mean is a requisite of a Zen house.  
It is natural to evaluate the material and give an assignment, 
But how do you understand those who are born of the same tree trunk and are of the same spirit?

When Ungan was sweeping the ground, Dôgo said, “You are having a hard time!”  Ungan said, “You should know there is one who doesn't have a hard time.”  Dôgo said, “If that's true, you mean there is a second moon?”  Ungan held up his broom and said, “What number of moon is this?”  Dôgo was silent.  
Gensha said, “That is precisely the second moon.”  
Unmon said, “The servant greets the maid politely.”

Taking up the subject, they easily have swept off the gates;
They have used it properly and now they rest.
The one that handled the Snake in front of the Elephant-Bone Rock44 –
Are you ashamed of your action of childhood when you are old?
text.uk: Майстер мовив: «Помри великою смертю. Тоді живи великим життям.»

author: Wanshi Shogaku (Hongzhi Zhengjue) / Wansong Xingxiu
source: Book of Equanimity / Shoyo-roku (1224), transl. Sanbo Kyodan Society

text.en:
Human beings are examined with words, water is checked with a stick.
Sweeping grasses and witnessing the wind – this is what is normally applied.
What if all of a sudden a tiger with a burned tail springs out?
